newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rebels say Chechnya secure despite priests' kidnap.
newsitem.headline: Rebels say Chechnya secure despite priests' kidnap.

text.p: Chechnya's interim rebel government said on Saturday that law and order were improving in the breakaway region ahead of this month's elections despite the kidnapping of two Russian Orthodox priests.

Interior Minister Kazbek Makhashev, echoing other leading separatists, told a news conference "certain forces" were bent on disrupting the elections and said the seizure of the priests on Thursday was another example of such "provocation".

"The situation is completely under control on the territory of Chechnya despite certain reports from the Russian media and other sources that speak of an extremely difficult criminal atmosphere here," he said.
"I must emphasise that recently there has been a sharp drop in crime, especially serious crimes like murder."
He said the average daily number of registered crimes in the tiny, war-ravaged region of one million fell from around 15 in December to less than 10 in the first part of January.

The two missing priests, who served Chechnya's much reduced ethnic Russian population, were abducted after being driven west of the capital Grozny to look for the grave of another Orthodox clergyman slain last year, Makhashev said.

The priests' Chechen driver was being interrogated but few details were yet known, he added. One of the abducted men, Father Yefimy, is the successor of the murdered priest in charge of Grozny's Church of St Michael the Archangel.

Patriarch Alexiy II, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, appealed for help from local Moslem clergy in securing the release of two two men, Itar-Tass news agency said. He noted his "particular sadness" that the "blasphemous deed" was carried out on the first day of the Moslem holy month of Ramadan.
"God grant that it should not set the followers of Christianity and Islam against one another," the patriarch said.
Makhashev said the abduction was deliberately designed to unsettle Russians still living in Chechnya. Many of the 300,000 living there before war broke out in December 1994 have fled.
"There are certain forces keen to undermine the rule of law and to show that the elections are not being carried out in line with the proper international standards," Makhashev said.

Last August a peace deal between Moscow and the Chechen rebels halted 21 months of bloody fighting in the southern region. Russia announced last week it had withdrawn all its troops from Chechnya, in line with the peace accord.
But security remains a key concern in the run-up to the presidential and parliamentary votes on January 27, especially since the murder of six foreign Red Cross workers last month.

One of the presidential candidates, information minister Movladi Udugov, said he believed rogue elements in Russia's security services were responsible for the killings, which led to the withdrawal of most foreign aid workers from Chechnya.
Makhashev, speaking in his office in central Grozny, said his ministry had taken a range of special measures to ensure the safety of international election observers and journalists.

"If there are further incidents they will also be aimed at trying to sabotage the elections," he added. Behind him hung a large green, white and red Chechen flag, on his desk was a picture of Dzhokhar Dudayev, late architect of Chechen secession.

Ordinary Chechens say they feel safe walking the streets even at night but the few remaining Russians keep a fairly low profile. "I only travel by car and never venture out at night," one told Reuters, asking not to be named.
Chechens linked to the now ousted pro-Moscow government of Doku Zavgayev also stay mostly at home for fear of reprisals.
